intro: Participles as adjectives, made into a two-way skill. Partizip I (infinitive + -d) = happening now, active: das lachende Kind, der ankommende Zug. Partizip II = done, mostly passive: das zerbrochene Fenster, die eingeladenen Gäste. Both take full adjective endings by article, gender and case. What this step adds is the extended form — the participle with its own complements in front of it: der um acht Uhr ankommende Zug, die von der Firma eingeladenen Gäste. This quiz drills the transformation in both directions. Folding: take a relative clause (der Zug, der um acht Uhr ankommt), move its complements in front of the verb, turn the verb into a participle, and give it the ending the article demands (der um acht Uhr ankommende Zug). Unfolding: read the phrase from the article to the noun, then rebuild the relative clause with the right pronoun, tense and voice (die Gäste, die von der Firma eingeladen wurden). A later module then drills the participle form alone inside longer attributes; here the whole phrase is yours to build.
tips[0].title: Partizip I: -end + ending (active, now)
tips[0].text: lachen → lachend: das lachende Kind · untergehen → die untergehende Sonne · ankommen → der ankommende Zug · blühen → die blühenden Blumen · bellen → der bellende Hund. = a relative clause with the present: der Hund, der bellt.
tips[0].check.why: Something happening right now is Partizip I, schlafend, and after das in the accusative neuter it takes the ending -e: das schlafende Baby.
tips[1].title: Partizip II: ge-…-t / -en + ending (done, passive)
tips[1].text: kochen → ein gekochtes Ei · bügeln → ein gebügeltes Hemd · zerbrechen → das zerbrochene Fenster · einladen → die eingeladenen Gäste · parken → das geparkte Auto. = a relative clause in the passive or Perfekt: das Fenster, das zerbrochen wurde / ist.
tips[1].trap: the participle is an adjective and must carry the ending: ein gekochtes Ei, not ein gekocht Ei; die eingeladenen Gäste, plural -en.
tips[1].check.why: The bike has been repaired, so it is Partizip II, and after sein in the neuter accusative the adjective needs -es: sein repariertes Fahrrad.
tips[2].title: Folding: complements first, then the participle, then the ending
tips[2].text: der Zug, der um acht Uhr ankommt → der um acht Uhr ankommende Zug · die Gäste, die von der Firma eingeladen wurden → die von der Firma eingeladenen Gäste. Everything from the relative clause except the pronoun and the auxiliary goes in front of the participle; the participle wears the adjective ending. Active present → Partizip I; passive or completed → Partizip II.
tips[2].check.why: Active and present means Partizip I, and the complement an der Kasse moves in front of the participle, which sits right before the noun.
tips[2].visual.rows[0].a: der Zug, der um acht ankommt
tips[2].visual.rows[2].a: die Kinder, die im Garten spielen
tips[3].title: Unfolding: pronoun, complements, verb — with tense and voice
tips[3].text: die von der Firma eingeladenen Gäste → die Gäste, die von der Firma eingeladen wurden (Partizip II → passive, past). der um acht Uhr ankommende Zug → der Zug, der um acht Uhr ankommt (Partizip I → active, present). Choose the relative pronoun by the noun (der / die / das), keep the complements, put the verb last.
tips[3].trap: A Partizip II attribute of a transitive verb unfolds into a passive (das gelesene Buch → das Buch, das gelesen wurde) or into an active clause with the agent as subject (das Buch, das ich gelesen habe). Both are right; the participle alone does not tell you who did it.
tips[3].check.why: Partizip II of a transitive verb unfolds into a passive in the past, and plural Briefe takes the relative pronoun die.
tips[4].title: -end = -ing, ge- = -ed, then the ending
tips[4].text: kochend = boiling, gekocht = boiled; add the adjective ending and you have both German forms.
tips[4].check.why: -end is the English -ing: fallend = falling. Gefallen would be 'fallen', already on the ground. After die in the plural the ending is -en.
remember[0]: Fold: complements → participle → ending. Unfold: pronoun → complements → verb last.
remember[1]: Partizip I = active, now; Partizip II = passive or done — that decides the tense and voice of the relative clause.
mistakes[0].why: Complements go before the participle, the participle before the noun.
mistakes[1].why: The participle is an adjective and needs the ending (-en after die, plural).
mistakes[2].why: Unfolding a Partizip II gives a passive: Partizip II + wurden.
hook: Fold 'the train that arrives at eight' into der um acht Uhr ankommende Zug, and unfold such phrases when reading.
recall.known: From "Partizip I & II als Adjektiv": das lachende Kind, das gekochte Ei.
recall.today: Folding a whole relative clause into the participle, and unfolding it again.
